name: Ezekiel

overview.author: Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest taken to Babylon in 597 BC with King Jehoiachin (1:1–3).
overview.date: Ezekiel’s visions are dated from 593 BC to 571 BC.
overview.audience: Jewish exiles in Babylon by the Chebar canal, who doubted God’s justice and clung to hope that Jerusalem could not fall.
overview.setting: Babylon. The first half is before Jerusalem’s fall (586 BC), and the second half comes after news of its destruction reaches the exiles (33:21).
overview.purpose: To show that Jerusalem’s fall was God’s just judgment, call individuals to repentance, and promise a new heart, a new David, a renewed people, and God’s glory dwelling with them again.
overview.structure: Ezekiel’s call (1–3), judgment on Judah and Jerusalem (4–24), oracles against the nations (25–32), and restoration (33–48), ending with the vision of a new temple.

items.title: Israel’s history of rebellion and the final siege
The watchman and the good shepherd
A new heart and dry bones
The new temple and the glory returns

themes.title: The Glory of God
themes.text: God’s glory appears to Ezekiel, departs from the temple, and returns to the new temple.

themes.title: “Then They Will Know That I Am the LORD”
themes.text: This refrain, used over 60 times, shows God’s purpose to make Himself known.

themes.title: God’s Holiness
themes.text: Israel’s idolatry defiled God’s name, and God acts for His holy name’s sake.

themes.title: Personal Responsibility
themes.text: “The soul who sins shall die” (18:4), and God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.

themes.title: The Watchman
themes.text: Ezekiel must warn the wicked; silence makes him accountable.

themes.title: New Heart and New Spirit
themes.text: God promises to remove the heart of stone and put His Spirit within (36:26–27).

themes.title: The Good Shepherd
themes.text: God Himself will shepherd His flock through His servant David (34).

themes.title: Resurrection and Renewal
themes.text: Dry bones live by the Spirit, and a river flows from the temple bringing life.

keyVerses.quote: For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live.
Turn back, turn back from your evil ways, for why will you die, O house of Israel?
I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out.
And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you.
Behold, I will cause breath to enter you, and you shall live.
And the name of the city from that time on shall be, The LORD Is There.

christInBook.text: God as the shepherd who seeks the lost is fulfilled in Jesus, the Good Shepherd (John 10:11; Luke 19:10).
The promise of cleansing water and the Spirit underlies Jesus’ words to Nicodemus (John 3:5).
“David my servant” as eternal king points to Jesus, the Son of David.
The likeness of a man on the throne foreshadows the glorified Son (Revelation 1:13–17).
The river of life flowing from the temple echoes Jesus’ living water (John 7:37–39; Revelation 22:1–2).

crossReferences.note: Born of water and the Spirit.
The throne vision with living creatures.
The new Jerusalem and the river of life.

reflection: Ezekiel saw God’s glory and fell on his face. When did you last stand in awe of God’s holiness?
Who has God placed you as a “watchman” for (3:17; 33:7)?
How does 18:23, 32 reveal God’s heart toward sinners, including you?
Where do you need God to replace a heart of stone with a heart of flesh (36:26)?
What “dry bones” in your life or community need the breath of God’s Spirit?

chapterList.title: The Vision of God’s Glory
chapterList.summary: By the Chebar canal in Babylon the heavens open, and Ezekiel sees a storm, four living creatures with four faces, wheels full of eyes, and above them a throne with the likeness of a man glowing like fire, surrounded by a rainbow. “Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD.” Ezekiel falls on his face.
questions: Why would God show Ezekiel His glory in exile?
What do the wheels and eyes suggest about God?
How does Revelation 4 echo this vision?

chapterList.title: Ezekiel’s Commission
chapterList.summary: The Spirit sets Ezekiel on his feet, and God sends him to rebellious Israel. “Whether they hear or refuse to hear,” they will know a prophet has been among them. He must not fear them. God gives him a scroll of lamentation and woe to eat.
questions: What did God tell Ezekiel to expect?
Why does God say not to be afraid (2:6)?
What does it mean that success is faithfulness, not results?

chapterList.title: The Watchman
chapterList.summary: Ezekiel eats the scroll, and it tastes like honey. God makes his forehead as hard as the people’s. He is appointed a watchman: if he fails to warn the wicked, their blood is on his hands. God then makes Ezekiel mute except when speaking God’s words.
questions: How did the scroll taste, and why (3:3)?
What is a watchman’s responsibility (3:17–21)?
Who are you responsible to warn and encourage?

chapterList.title: The Siege Enacted
chapterList.summary: Ezekiel acts out the siege of Jerusalem with a brick and an iron plate. He lies on his left side 390 days and on his right side 40 days for Israel’s and Judah’s sins, eating rationed bread cooked over dung.
questions: Why might God use visual dramas to communicate?
What do the days represent?
What does the rationed food teach about the coming siege?

chapterList.title: The Shaved Hair
chapterList.summary: Ezekiel shaves his head and beard and divides the hair: a third burned, a third struck with the sword, a third scattered. A few hairs bound in his robe represent a remnant. Jerusalem’s sin exceeded the nations’.
questions: What did the divided hair symbolize?
Why was Jerusalem’s sin worse than the nations’ (5:6–7)?
What does the small remnant teach about God’s mercy?

chapterList.title: Against the Mountains of Israel
chapterList.summary: God declares judgment on the high places where Israel worshiped idols. Yet a remnant will remember Him and loathe themselves for their evil. “And they shall know that I am the LORD.”
questions: What were the high places?
How does judgment lead to self-knowledge (6:9)?
What does it mean to “know that I am the LORD”?

chapterList.title: The End Has Come
chapterList.summary: “An end has come upon the four corners of the land.” God’s wrath will be poured out. Silver and gold cannot save them in the day of the LORD’s wrath; they become a stumbling block.
questions: Why is the repetition of “the end” so dramatic?
Why can’t wealth save on the day of wrath (7:19)?
What warning does this give to us?

chapterList.title: Abominations in the Temple
chapterList.summary: Ezekiel is carried in a vision to Jerusalem’s temple, where he sees an image of jealousy, elders burning incense to creeping things, women weeping for Tammuz, and men worshiping the sun with their backs to the temple.
questions: What idolatry was hidden in the temple?
Why did the elders think “The LORD does not see us” (8:12)?
What hidden idols might lurk in our hearts?

chapterList.title: The Mark on the Foreheads
chapterList.summary: God sends a man with a writing case to mark those who sigh and groan over the city’s abominations. Executioners kill the rest, beginning at the sanctuary. Ezekiel cries out, but God says their guilt is exceedingly great.
questions: Who received the mark, and why?
Why does judgment begin at God’s sanctuary (9:6)?
How does Revelation echo the sealing of God’s people?

chapterList.title: The Glory Leaves the Temple
chapterList.summary: Coals from between the cherubim are scattered over the city. The glory of the LORD rises from the threshold of the temple and stands over the cherubim, preparing to depart.
questions: What does the departure of God’s glory mean?
Why is this one of the saddest moments in the Old Testament?
How does God’s glory return in Jesus (John 1:14)?

chapterList.title: A New Heart Promised
chapterList.summary: Ezekiel denounces leaders giving wicked counsel, and one, Pelatiah, dies. God promises to be a sanctuary for the exiles and give them “one heart” and “a new spirit,” removing the heart of stone. The glory departs to the mountain east of the city.
questions: How was God a sanctuary to the exiles (11:16)?
What does God promise in 11:19–20?
Where does the glory go (11:23), and why is this significant (Acts 1:11–12)?

chapterList.title: The Exile Enacted
chapterList.summary: Ezekiel packs an exile’s baggage and digs through a wall at night as a sign of the coming captivity and the prince’s flight. People say visions are delayed, but God says, “None of my words will be delayed any longer.”
questions: How was this fulfilled in Zedekiah’s flight (2 Kings 25:4–7)?
Why did people think the visions would never come true (12:22, 27)?
How does 2 Peter 3:3–9 answer similar doubts today?

chapterList.title: False Prophets
chapterList.summary: God condemns prophets who follow their own spirit, saying “Peace” when there is no peace, like those who whitewash a flimsy wall. He also condemns women who use magic bands to hunt souls.
questions: What does “whitewashing a wall” picture?
How do false teachers discourage the righteous and encourage the wicked (13:22)?
How can you discern true from false teaching?

chapterList.title: Idols in the Heart
chapterList.summary: Elders who have taken idols into their hearts come to inquire of God. God says even Noah, Daniel, and Job could not save the land by their righteousness, only themselves.
questions: What does it mean to take idols into the heart (14:3)?
Why mention Noah, Daniel, and Job?
Why can’t anyone be saved by another’s righteousness except Christ’s?

chapterList.title: The Useless Vine
chapterList.summary: Jerusalem is like a vine’s wood, good for nothing but burning. Since it bore no fruit, it will be given to the fire.
questions: Why is a vine good only for fruit?
How does Jesus use the vine image (John 15:1–6)?
What fruit is God looking for in you?

chapterList.title: The Unfaithful Bride
chapterList.summary: God tells Jerusalem’s story: an abandoned baby He rescued, raised, married, and adorned. But she trusted in her beauty and played the whore with idols and nations. God will judge her, yet He will remember His covenant and establish an everlasting covenant and atone for her.
questions: What does the story show about God’s grace (16:4–14)?
How did Jerusalem respond to that grace?
How does 16:60–63 end with hope?

chapterList.title: Two Eagles and a Vine
chapterList.summary: A riddle of two eagles and a vine pictures Zedekiah breaking his oath to Babylon and turning to Egypt. God will punish him, but God Himself will plant a tender sprig on a high mountain, which will become a noble cedar sheltering birds.
questions: Why is breaking an oath so serious to God?
Who is the tender sprig God plants (17:22–24)?
How does Jesus’ mustard seed parable echo this?

chapterList.title: The Soul Who Sins Shall Die
chapterList.summary: The exiles quote a proverb: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.” God rejects it: each person is responsible. The righteous who turns to evil dies; the wicked who turns lives. “Make yourselves a new heart... For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone... so turn, and live.”
questions: Why was the proverb a way of avoiding responsibility?
What does God desire for sinners (18:23, 32)?
How does this chapter call you to personal repentance?

chapterList.title: A Lament for Israel’s Princes
chapterList.summary: A lament pictures Judah’s kings as young lions captured and taken to Egypt and Babylon, and Judah as a vine uprooted and burned.
questions: Which kings are described as captured lions?
What does the uprooted vine represent?
Why does God give laments to His prophets?

chapterList.title: Israel’s Rebellious History
chapterList.summary: Elders come to inquire, and God recounts Israel’s rebellion in Egypt, the wilderness, and the land. Yet repeatedly God acted “for the sake of my name.” He will purge rebels and bring His people out with a mighty hand, and they will know He is the LORD.
questions: Why does God keep acting “for the sake of my name”?
What role did the Sabbath play (20:12)?
How does God’s faithfulness exceed Israel’s faithlessness?

chapterList.title: The Sword of the LORD
chapterList.summary: God draws His sword against Jerusalem. The king of Babylon chooses Jerusalem by divination at a fork in the road. The crown will be removed “until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs.”
questions: Why would God’s own sword be against His people?
Who is “he... to whom judgment belongs” (21:27)?
How does Genesis 49:10 relate?

chapterList.title: The Bloody City
chapterList.summary: Jerusalem’s sins are listed: bloodshed, idolatry, contempt for parents, oppression of foreigners, orphans, and widows, profaning the Sabbath, sexual sin, and bribery. Princes, priests, prophets, and people are all corrupt. God sought a man to “stand in the breach,” but found none.
questions: Which sins in 22:6–12 stand out to you?
Who failed in their responsibilities (22:25–29)?
How did Jesus become the one who stands in the breach?

chapterList.title: Oholah and Oholibah
chapterList.summary: Two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), prostitute themselves with Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt. Jerusalem saw Samaria’s judgment yet became more corrupt. She will drink her sister’s cup.
questions: What do the two sisters represent?
Why didn’t Jerusalem learn from Samaria’s judgment?
How does political trust become spiritual unfaithfulness?

chapterList.title: The Boiling Pot and Ezekiel’s Wife
chapterList.summary: On the day Babylon besieges Jerusalem, God gives Ezekiel a parable of a rusted pot. Then Ezekiel’s wife, “the delight of your eyes,” dies, and God tells him not to mourn publicly, as a sign that Jerusalem’s temple will be lost.
questions: What does the rust in the pot represent?
How costly was Ezekiel’s obedience?
What was the people meant to learn from Ezekiel’s silence?

chapterList.title: Against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and Philistia
chapterList.summary: God judges Israel’s neighbors for rejoicing over Jerusalem’s fall and taking revenge. “They shall know that I am the LORD.”
questions: What sin do these nations share?
Why does God care how others treat His people?
How does Proverbs 24:17 warn against gloating?

chapterList.title: Against Tyre
chapterList.summary: Tyre rejoices at Jerusalem’s fall, expecting gain. God will bring Nebuchadnezzar against it; Tyre will become a bare rock for drying nets.
questions: Why did Tyre gloat over Jerusalem?
How was this prophecy fulfilled over time?
What does this teach about trusting wealth?

chapterList.title: A Lament for Tyre
chapterList.summary: Tyre is pictured as a magnificent merchant ship, laden with goods from many nations, that sinks in the heart of the sea. Sailors and merchants mourn.
questions: What made Tyre so impressive?
How does Revelation 18 echo this lament?
Why is commercial greatness so fragile?

chapterList.title: The King of Tyre
chapterList.summary: The prince of Tyre says, “I am a god.” God answers that he is but a man. A lament describes the king of Tyre as once in Eden, a guardian cherub, blameless until pride corrupted him and he was cast down. God promises to gather Israel and let them dwell securely.
questions: How does pride lead to self-deification?
Why do many see Satan’s fall reflected in 28:12–17?
What promise closes the chapter (28:25–26)?

chapterList.title: Against Egypt
chapterList.summary: Pharaoh claims the Nile as his own creation. God will hook him like a sea monster and make Egypt a lowly kingdom. Egypt had been a broken reed for Israel. God gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as wages.
questions: What was Pharaoh’s pride (29:3, 9)?
Why was Egypt a “staff of reed” for Israel (29:6–7)?
How does God use even Nebuchadnezzar’s labor?

chapterList.title: The Day of the LORD for Egypt
chapterList.summary: A day of the LORD is near for Egypt and its allies. God breaks Pharaoh’s arms and strengthens Babylon’s.
questions: What does breaking Pharaoh’s arms mean?
How does God direct the strength of nations?
What does “the day of the LORD” mean here?

chapterList.title: The Fallen Cedar
chapterList.summary: Pharaoh is compared to Assyria, once a towering cedar in God’s garden, envied by Eden’s trees, but cut down for its pride and sent down to Sheol.
questions: Why compare Egypt to Assyria?
What does the fall of the great cedar teach?
How does pride lead to downfall?

chapterList.title: Lament for Pharaoh
chapterList.summary: A lament for Pharaoh, a sea monster caught in God’s net. Egypt joins Assyria, Elam, Meshech, Edom, and others in the pit, the realm of the dead, among those who spread terror.
questions: What is the scene in the pit (32:17–32)?
How does death humble the powerful?
What hope do believers have that these nations lacked?

chapterList.title: The Watchman and the Fall of Jerusalem
chapterList.summary: God renews Ezekiel’s role as watchman and declares, “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked... turn back... why will you die?” A fugitive arrives: “The city has been struck down.” The people enjoy Ezekiel’s preaching like a love song but do not obey.
questions: What does 33:11 reveal about God’s heart?
Why does news of the fall matter for Ezekiel’s ministry?
How might we treat preaching like entertainment (33:31–32)?

chapterList.title: The Good Shepherd
chapterList.summary: God condemns Israel’s shepherds, who fed themselves instead of the sheep. “I, I myself will search for my sheep.” He will seek the lost, bind the injured, and judge between sheep. He will set over them one shepherd, “my servant David,” and make a covenant of peace.
questions: What did the bad shepherds fail to do (34:4)?
How does God promise to shepherd (34:11–16)?
How is Jesus this shepherd (John 10:11–16)?

chapterList.title: Against Mount Seir
chapterList.summary: Edom (Mount Seir) is judged for its perpetual enmity toward Israel, handing Israel over in its calamity and wanting to possess its land.
questions: What was Edom’s ongoing sin?
How does God hear the words spoken against His people (35:12–13)?
How does Obadiah echo this oracle?

chapterList.title: A New Heart and a New Spirit
chapterList.summary: God will restore the mountains of Israel, not for Israel’s sake but for His holy name. “I will sprinkle clean water on you... And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you... And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes.”
questions: Why does God act for His name’s sake (36:22–23)?
What does the new heart and Spirit accomplish (36:26–27)?
How does Jesus refer to this in John 3:5?

chapterList.title: The Valley of Dry Bones
chapterList.summary: In a valley of dry bones, God asks, “Son of man, can these bones live?” Ezekiel prophesies, the bones come together, and the breath enters them; they stand as an exceedingly great army. Two sticks joined in one hand picture a reunited Israel under one king, David, with an everlasting covenant and God’s dwelling place among them.
questions: What do the dry bones represent (37:11)?
How does the Spirit give life (37:14)?
How does 37:24–28 point to Christ and His church?

chapterList.title: Gog of Magog
chapterList.summary: Gog, from the land of Magog, leads a vast coalition against restored Israel, living in security. God brings Gog against His land to show His holiness and then shakes the earth and destroys Gog’s armies.
questions: Why does God say He brings Gog (38:16)?
What does this vision teach about God’s protection of His people?
How does Revelation 20:7–10 use Gog and Magog?

chapterList.title: Gog’s Defeat
chapterList.summary: Gog’s armies fall, and Israel spends seven months burying them and seven years burning their weapons. God will restore Israel and pour out His Spirit on them, never again hiding His face.
questions: How long are weapons burned, and what does that suggest?
Why did God hide His face in the past (39:23–24)?
What does 39:29 promise?

chapterList.title: The Vision of the New Temple
chapterList.summary: Twenty-five years into exile, Ezekiel is taken in a vision to a very high mountain and shown a new temple by a man with a measuring rod. The gates, courts, and chambers are measured in detail.
questions: Why would detailed measurements encourage exiles?
How does Revelation 21 use similar imagery?
What does the temple tell us about God’s desire to dwell with His people?

chapterList.title: The Temple’s Inner Sanctuary
chapterList.summary: The man measures the nave and the Most Holy Place and describes the carved cherubim and palm trees on the walls, and the wooden altar, “the table that is before the LORD.”
questions: What does the Most Holy Place represent?
How does Jesus open the way into God’s presence (Hebrews 10:19–22)?
Why are cherubim and palm trees, images of Eden, carved there?

chapterList.title: The Priests’ Chambers
chapterList.summary: Chambers for the priests are measured, where they eat the holy offerings and change garments. The outer wall separates the holy from the common.
questions: Why did the temple have walls separating holy from common?
What does it mean that believers are now a holy priesthood (1 Peter 2:9)?
How should we treat what is holy?

chapterList.title: The Glory Returns
chapterList.summary: The glory of the God of Israel comes from the east, the earth shining with His glory, and fills the temple. God says, “This is the place of my throne... where I will dwell in the midst of the people of Israel forever.” The altar is described and consecrated.
questions: How does this scene reverse chapters 10–11?
What does God promise in 43:7?
How does the glory return in Christ and in the new creation?

chapterList.title: The Closed Gate and the Priests
chapterList.summary: The east gate is shut because the LORD has entered by it. Foreigners and unfaithful Levites are excluded from priestly service, but the sons of Zadok, who remained faithful, will minister and teach the people the difference between holy and common.
questions: Why is the gate shut (44:2)?
Why were Zadok’s sons honored?
What is a priest’s teaching role (44:23)?

chapterList.title: Allotments and Offerings
chapterList.summary: A holy district is set apart for the sanctuary, priests, Levites, and the prince. God demands just weights and measures. Offerings are prescribed for the feasts.
questions: Why does God require honest scales (45:10)?
How does God restrain the prince’s power (45:8–9)?
What do the feasts celebrate?

chapterList.title: Worship of the Prince and People
chapterList.summary: Rules for worship on Sabbaths, new moons, and feasts are given. People must exit by the opposite gate from the one they entered. The prince’s inheritance must not be taken from the people.
questions: Why must people leave by the opposite gate (46:9)?
What might that picture about meeting God?
How does God protect the people’s inheritance (46:18)?

chapterList.title: The River from the Temple
chapterList.summary: Water flows from under the temple, getting deeper until it is a river that cannot be crossed. Wherever it flows, it brings life, even to the Dead Sea. Trees on its banks bear fruit every month, with leaves for healing. The land’s boundaries are set, and foreigners receive an inheritance.
questions: What does the river represent?
How does Jesus speak of rivers of living water (John 7:37–39)?
How does Revelation 22:1–2 complete this picture?

chapterList.title: The LORD Is There
chapterList.summary: The land is divided among the twelve tribes, with the holy portion in the center. The city has twelve gates named for the tribes. Its name will be “The LORD Is There.”
questions: Why is the city’s name the climax of the book?
How does Revelation 21:12–14 echo the twelve gates?
What does God’s presence mean for your hope?

tagline: The glory departs and returns: “Then they will know that I am the LORD”
readingPlan: 48 chapters: one chapter a day takes 48 days; two a day takes about 24 days. For each chapter, read it on ESV.org, then come back here for the summary, questions, and your notes.
